Become
bē-kŭm'
v. (to come to be; to pass into a state — in Scripture the verb of the new birth, the new creature, and the rejected stone)
From Anglo-Saxon becuman — be- (about) plus cuman (to come): literally to come about, to arrive at a condition. The sense of to befit (as in it becomes a man) is a later branch of the same word.

Biblical Definition

Become is the verb of transformation, and the New Testament reserves it for God's work. It states the right of sonship: “as many as received him, to them gave he power to become the sons of God, even to them that believe on his name” (Joh 1:12) — and the next verse rules out any human contribution, since such are born “not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God”. It states the new creation: “if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new” (2Co 5:17). It states the required reversal: “Except ye be converted, and become as little children, ye shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven” (Mat 18:3) — where the childlikeness in view is dependence and lowliness, not innocence, since children are not innocent. And it states the great reversal of the builders' verdict: “The stone which the builders refused is become the head stone of the corner” (Psa 118:22), the verse the Lord Jesus applied to Himself and Peter preached before the Sanhedrin.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines become as to pass from one state to another, to enter into some state or condition — and, transitively, to suit or be suitable to, to befit.

expand to see more

BECOME, v.i. To pass from one state to another; to enter into some state or condition, by a change from another state.

The Lord God breathed into his nostrils the breath of life, and man became a living soul. Gen. ii.

2. To become of, usually with what preceding; to be the fate of; to be the end of.

BECOME, v.t. To suit; to be suitable to; to befit; to accord with, in character or circumstances.

Holiness becometh thy house, O Lord, for ever. Ps. xciii.

Key Scripture

Joh 1:12 — "But as many as received him, to them gave he power to become the sons of God, even to them that believe on his name:"

2Co 5:17 — "Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new."

Mat 18:3 — "And said, Verily I say unto you, Except ye be converted, and become as little children, ye shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven."

Psa 118:22 — "The stone which the builders refused is become the head stone of the corner."

Modern Corruption

Joh 1:12 is read as though the power to become sons lay in the human decision, and Mat 18:3 is sentimentalised into a doctrine of childhood innocence.

expand to see more

“To them gave he power to become the sons of God” is regularly preached as the charter of decisional religion: God supplies the option, man supplies the choice. John himself excludes that reading in the very next sentence, which specifies that those who so believe “were born, not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God”. Three human sources of new birth are named and all three are denied. The receiving and believing are real and are the believer's own acts; their origin is not. That is the monergism of the new birth, and it is stated by the same apostle who records the Lord telling Nicodemus that a man must be born again to see the kingdom at all.

Mat 18:3 is likewise softened into a tribute to the innocence of children, which Scripture nowhere teaches — “foolishness is bound in the heart of a child” (Pro 22:15), and David says he was shapen in iniquity. The context supplies the actual point: the disciples had been arguing who should be greatest, and the Lord sets a child in the midst and says the greatest is he who humbles himself as this little child. What is commended is smallness, dependence, and the absence of any claim to rank. That is a harder word to the ambitious than a compliment to childhood, and it is the one He gave.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Anglo-Saxon becuman, to come about; rendering Hebrew hayah (H1961), to be, become, come to pass, and Greek ginomai (G1096), to become, come into being.

expand to see more

Anglo-Saxon becuman — be- about + cuman to come; to arrive at a state.

Hebrew hayah (H1961) — to be, become, come to pass; “man became a living soul” (Gen 2:7) and “is become the head stone” (Psa 118:22).

Greek ginomai (G1096) — to come into being, become; distinct from eimi, to be — a distinction John exploits in his prologue, where the Word was and all things were made.

Joh 1:12 — exousian genesthai tekna theou, authority or right to become children of God; exousia is warrant, not raw capability.

Greek kaine ktisis (2Co 5:17) — a new creation; kainos is new in kind, not merely new in time.

Usage

"“Power to become the sons of God” — a right conferred, and a birth not of the will of man."

"“All things are become new” — new in kind, not merely recent."

"“Is become the head stone of the corner” — the builders' verdict overturned."
